guides.title: Basket or oven-style air fryer: what should you compare?
guides.description: Basket and oven-style air fryers are different tools. Here is what actually changes between them, using manufacturer specifications from three units compared side by side.
guides.image_alt: A basket air fryer drawer of golden fries beside a small countertop oven holding a tray of roasted vegetables.
guides.deck: The shape decides more than the brand does. Start with the food you cook most, then compare the three numbers that actually differ.

body.text: Two air fryers can hold the same number of quarts and still cook very differently, because a basket and a countertop oven are not the same machine with a different shell. One has a drawer you pull out and shake. The other has a door, racks, and heat coming from more than one direction. Most buying advice skips this and starts with brands.
What actually changes between the two shapes

A basket fryer moves hot air over food sitting in a single perforated drawer. You pull the drawer, shake, and push it back. An oven-style unit puts food on a rack or tray inside a box with a door, so you can use more than one level and you can put a pan in it. That single difference drives everything else: how much fits, how evenly it browns, how much counter it eats, and how much of it you can put in a dishwasher.

body.caption: Three units, manufacturer specifications only. A dash means the manufacturer page did not state it.
rows: Oven with french doors and racks
Yes, interior light and glass doors

body.text: Those four specification rows come from each manufacturer's own product page, fetched on 2026-11-20. Where the page is silent the cell stays blank rather than borrowing a number from a retailer listing. The full row-by-row record, including the Amazon pages each product resolved to, is on the Shop table.
Question one: are you cooking two things at once?

If dinner is usually a main and a side that need different temperatures, a dual basket is the smallest thing that solves it. The CHEFMAN 6 Qt gives you two independent 3-quart drawers, and its Sync Finish setting runs both timers so they land together (S11). That is a real convenience, and it is the reason this shape exists.

The catch is arithmetic. Two 3-quart baskets are each half the size of one 6-quart drawer, so a single big batch of fries gets split across two drawers and you still end up shaking both. If your cooking is mostly one big pile of one thing, the extra basket buys you nothing.
Question two: how much of the counter can you give up?

This is where the oven shape loses. The Emeril Lagasse 26 Qt measures 16.9 inches deep, 15.8 wide and 14.8 tall by the manufacturer's own figures (S13). That is not a small appliance, and it needs clearance for a door that swings toward you. A basket unit at 13.38 x 11.81 x 10.63 inches (S11) sits in a corner and gets pushed back when you are done.

If you have a small kitchen, measure the depth of your counter before anything else. A deep oven-style unit that has to live on the dining table will annoy you every day, and no amount of capacity makes up for that.
Question three: do you want to see the food, or open the drawer?

The dual-basket Chefman has a window on each basket and an interior light (S11), so checking on food does not dump the heat. The TurboFry 8 Qt does not list a window at all; checking means pulling the basket, which is exactly when the heat leaves. This sounds like a small thing until it is the fourth time you have opened it.
Windows are not a substitute for a rack, though. If you want to bake a 12-inch pizza or run a rotisserie, an oven-shaped box with a door is the only one of the three that can do it.
What none of these pages will tell you

None of the three manufacturer pages states how evenly the unit browns food, how loud the fan is, or how long it takes to come up to temperature. Those are the things a review is supposed to measure, and this site has not tested any of these units. What you are reading is a specification comparison, not a test.

Two more things are genuinely unresolved. The Emeril page gives conflicting preset counts (25 and 24 in the same page), and the Chefman 8 Qt Amazon listing carries a model-number field that does not match the manufacturer's model for this feature set. Both are recorded on the Flagged for review page rather than smoothed over.
A short version

items: Two foods, two timings, small kitchen: dual basket, and accept the smaller drawers.
One big pile of one thing, family portions: single large basket, and get one with a window if you can.
Whole meals, baking, rotisserie, and you have the counter depth: oven-style, measured before you buy.
No counter depth and no patience for batches: none of these. A sheet pan and a normal oven is cheaper.

guides.title: A no-hype checklist for comparing air fryer capacity
guides.description: Quarts are the easiest number to misread on an air fryer listing. Here is how to compare 6, 8 and 26 quart units honestly, including what the numbers do not tell you.
guides.image_alt: An overhead view of a parchment-lined air fryer basket with a small chicken, plates and a skillet arranged beside it for scale.
guides.deck: Capacity is the first number on the box and the easiest to misread. Five checks, in order.

body.text: A 6-quart air fryer and a 6-quart air fryer are not the same amount of usable space. One may spread that volume across two drawers; another may pour it into one deep bucket whose shape wastes the corners. Quarts are a volume, and volume is not a cooking surface.
1. Find out whether the number is total or per drawer

The CHEFMAN 6 Qt is 6 quarts total, delivered as two independent 3-quart baskets (S11). If you compare its '6' directly against a single-basket 8-quart unit, you are comparing one number that can only be used half at a time against one that cannot. Write down both figures before you compare anything.
2. Ask how much of the volume a single layer of food actually fills

Air frying depends on air moving around the food. A full basket that is packed to the rim browns unevenly, which is why most manuals tell you to work in batches. In practice the usable capacity of any of these units is the amount that fits in one layer with a little room to spare, and that is always less than the number printed on the box.

No manufacturer page reviewed for this site states a recommended maximum load in quarts or pounds, so there is no official number to quote here. What you can do is measure the flat area of the basket or rack, which is the number that decides whether your food fits.
3. Compare the shape, not just the size

Eight quarts in one basket (S12) is a different cooking experience from six quarts in two. The single basket takes a whole chicken or a big pile of fries; the dual basket takes two smaller piles that finish at different times. Neither is more capacity in any useful sense. They are two shapes of the same question.
4. Look at the footprint per quart

Divide the counter area by the quarts and the oven-style units stop looking generous. The Emeril Lagasse 26 Qt is 26 quarts but occupies 16.9 by 15.8 inches of counter, roughly 267 square inches (S13). The CHEFMAN 6 Qt occupies 13.38 by 11.81, roughly 158 square inches (S11). You are paying for the big one in kitchen real estate as well as money.
That is not an argument against the large unit. If you cook for six people, 26 quarts is the only number here that gets dinner on the table in one pass. It is an argument for measuring first.
5. Write down what the page did not say

The Chefman 8 Qt manufacturer page does not state overall dimensions, so this site shows none for that product. That is not an oversight to be filled in later from a marketplace listing; it is the honest state of the evidence. When a page is silent, the useful action is to note the gap and check the manual when the unit arrives.
The checklist, on one screen

items: Total quarts or per-basket quarts? Write both.
What fits in one layer with room for air to move?
Is the shape a single pile or two separate piles?
Square inches of counter per quart of capacity.
Which number on the page was missing, and where will you get it?

body.text: No capacity on this page is described as better. The units differ in what they are for; the checklist is only about reading the numbers honestly.

guides.title: How to assess cleanup and counter-space trade-offs
guides.description: Dishwasher claims, window designs and real counter footprints: how to judge the two costs nobody puts on the box, using manufacturer specifications.
guides.image_alt: A clean air fryer basket and crisper tray drying on a grey linen towel beside a soft brush and a bowl of soapy water.
guides.deck: You will clean this thing more often than you will admire it, and you will look at it every day. Both costs are knowable before you buy.

body.text: Two costs never make it onto the marketing photo: how much of your evening the cleanup takes, and how much of your counter the appliance permanently owns. Both can be judged from a manufacturer page if you know which sentences to look for.
Cleanup: read the dishwasher sentence carefully

There is a difference between 'dishwasher safe' and 'top rack dishwasher safe', and a further difference between the basket and the rest of the unit. The Chefman TurboFry 8 Qt page says the nonstick basket and rack are top-rack dishwasher safe (S12). The CHEFMAN 6 Qt page says its baskets are nonstick and dishwasher safe (S11). Neither page claims the housing can go in the sink, and no page reviewed here claims the heating element can be washed at all.

body.caption: What each manufacturer page actually claims about cleaning.
rows: Wipe clean only; no dishwasher claim
Basket and rack top-rack dishwasher safe
Manufacturer page makes no dishwasher claim

body.text: A blank in that table is not a defect in the product. It means the manufacturer has not published the claim, so this site does not assert it.
The second cost: the counter, measured two ways

Counter space has a footprint and a clearance. Footprint is the base of the unit; clearance is the room it needs to work. A basket fryer needs room in front of it for the drawer to slide out. An oven-style unit needs room for a door that opens toward you, and the Emeril's dimensions of 16.9 inches deep by 14.8 tall (S13) mean the door swing is not trivial.

Go stand at your counter with a tape measure. Mark the footprint with painter's tape, then open a cupboard door in the same space to represent the drawer or the oven door. This takes two minutes and settles arguments that product photos never will.
Windows and lights change how often you clean

A window with an interior light (S11) means you check on food without pulling the drawer. Every pull drops heat, and every drop in heat is a minute added at the end. The single-basket TurboFry 8 Qt does not list a window, so checking means opening it (S12). Over a year of cooking, that is a lot of extra openings, and a lot of extra time standing over the unit.
What nobody tells you about the corners

The awkward part of cleaning any air fryer is the corner where the basket meets the crisper plate, and the underside of the plate itself. A removable plate that lifts out is easier than one that is fixed into the drawer. None of the manufacturer pages reviewed here describes whether the crisper plate is removable, so that is a question for the manual or the box before you commit.
A practical order of operations

items: Find the dishwasher sentence on the manufacturer page and note exactly which parts it covers.
Measure the footprint on your counter with tape.
Test the drawer or door clearance with a cupboard door.
Decide whether a window is worth it to you. Then decide the size.

guides.title: Questions to ask before buying a multi-function kitchen appliance
guides.description: A 26-quart countertop oven promises air frying, baking, rotisserie and more. Six questions that separate the functions you will use from the ones on the box.
guides.image_alt: A kitchen table with an open blank notebook, a pencil, a mug and a whole chicken on a board.
guides.deck: Every function on the box is a function you have to store, clean and learn. Ask which ones you will actually use.

body.text: A multi-function countertop appliance is a bet that one machine can replace three. Sometimes it can. The honest way to decide is to count the functions you will use weekly, then check whether the unit does those well, rather than counting the functions on the front panel.
1. Which functions do you already perform weekly?

Write down what you cooked in the last two weeks. If the list is mostly toast, frozen fries and reheating leftovers, a large multi-function oven is a lot of cabinet to buy for three jobs a much smaller appliance already does. If the list includes a whole chicken, a tray of vegetables and a bake on the same evening, the case gets stronger.
2. Does the manufacturer agree with itself?

The Emeril Lagasse 26 Qt page states '25 Cooking Pre-sets' in its specification strip and '24 one-touch cooking presets' in its own product description, and an image on the same page reads '11-in-1' (S13). The Amazon listing for the same unit says 24 presets and six accessories, while the manufacturer text mentions seven. When a manufacturer cannot keep one number straight across one page, treat the preset count as marketing rather than specification.
That is why this site publishes no preset count for this unit. The conflict is logged as FLG-005 with both source links, so you can look at the same pages and decide for yourself.
3. How much counter does it actually take, with the door open?

The unit is 16.9 inches deep, 15.8 wide and 14.8 tall by the manufacturer's figures (S13). Add the door swing and the clearance behind it for the cord. If your counter is 24 inches deep, you have about 7 inches left in front of the unit when it is pushed back, which is not enough room to slide a hot tray out safely.
4. Which parts go in the dishwasher?

For this unit, the manufacturer page does not state a dishwasher claim for any part (S13). If easy cleanup is the reason you are buying a multi-function appliance, that omission matters more than any preset.
5. What is the failure mode?

A single machine that does five jobs is also a single point of failure for five jobs. If it dies, you lose the toaster and the oven at once. This is not an argument against the category; it is an argument for knowing which of your other appliances you would keep in the cupboard as a backup.
6. Has anyone tested it, or is this a spec sheet?

Everything on this page is a specification comparison drawn from the manufacturer's own product page, not a test. This site has not cooked in this unit, has not measured how evenly it browns, and does not know how loud the fan is. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. The point of the specification approach is that you can check every number yourself against the source link.
If you only ask one question

Ask which two functions you will use at least once a week. If the answer is 'air fry and reheat', buy the smallest air fryer that fits your food and keep your oven. If the answer is 'air fry and bake, for six people', the big unit starts to make sense.

guides.title: Is your meat thermometer telling you the right number?
guides.description: The USDA safe minimum temperatures, where to put the probe, and the difference between an instant-read spot check and a leave-in wireless probe.
guides.image_alt: A thin probe thermometer inserted into the thigh of a roast chicken resting in a cast-iron skillet.
guides.deck: A thermometer is only useful if the number is right, in the right place, compared against the right target.

body.text: Most complaints about meat thermometers are really complaints about one of three things: the probe was in the wrong spot, the reading was taken before the temperature had settled, or the cook had no reference number to compare against. All three are fixable before you spend anything.
Start with the number you are aiming for

The USDA Food Safety and Inspection Service publishes safe minimum internal temperatures, measured with a food thermometer before the food leaves the heat source. The ones that matter most for home cooking are below, quoted from the FSIS chart (S10).

body.caption: Safe minimum internal temperatures, quoted from the FSIS chart. Rest times are part of the instruction, not a suggestion.
rows: Beef, pork, veal, lamb steaks, chops, roasts

body.text: FSIS notes that these are minimums and that personal preference may lead you to cook higher. It also says to measure with a food thermometer, not by colour or by time.
Where to put the probe

For a whole bird, the thickest part of the thigh is a reliable spot, along with the thickest part of the breast, staying away from bone and from the cavity. Bone conducts heat differently and will give you a reading that is not the meat. For a roast, go into the centre of the thickest part, not the end.
Two kinds of thermometer, two different jobs

A leave-in probe stays in the meat and reports continuously. The CHEF iQ Sense uses four internal sensors and one ambient sensor, with an ambient range up to 1000 F, and relays readings through a Wi-Fi hub (S14). That ambient sensor is the part people skip: it tells you the temperature around the food, which is what actually drives cooking time and what catches a flare-up before it ruins the cook.

An instant-read probe is a spot check. You open the lid, stab, read, and close. It is faster to set up, it needs no app, and it cannot tell you anything while the lid is closed. Neither kind is better; they answer different questions.
The claims worth being sceptical about

Accuracy claims like plus or minus half a degree look impressive next to a safe-minimum table measured in whole degrees. They matter far less than probe placement and settling time. A perfectly accurate probe in the wrong spot is worse than an average probe in the right one, because it gives you a precise number you should not trust.

Two specific conflicts are recorded on the Flagged for review page: the CHEF iQ manufacturer's own pages disagree on battery life (70+ hours on one page, up to 60 on the FAQ), and the ThermoMaven unit has no manufacturer page at all, so none of its specifications are published here.
A 60-second calibration check

items: Fill a glass with crushed ice and water, stir, and wait a minute.
Insert the probe without touching the glass.
It should read close to 32 F. If it is far off, the probe is the problem, not your cooking.
Repeat at the start of the season, not the middle of a dinner party.
